newsitem.title: BELGIUM: More than 630,000 tap into EU.
newsitem.headline: More than 630,000 tap into EU.

text.p: More than 630,000 people have already taken advantage of a European Commission initiative to provide easy access to information about how to use and benefit from the European Union's border-free market.
The campaign -- dubbed Citizens First -- was launced six months ago to inform people in the 15-nation EU about their rights and opportunities in the single market.

It allows people to seek advice, for example, on how to live, work and study in other EU countries by accessing "http://citizens.EU.int", which the EU calls the world's biggest multilingual Web site on the Internet.
The site also contains pages in every European language on how to benefit from EU laws on health and safety at work, equal opportunities and consumer protection.
Those unable to surf the Internet can get information by dialing special telephone numbers in each of the EU countries.
"Over 230,000 have made telephone calls and some 400,000 people have downloaded more than 2.5 million documents from the Citizens First Internet site," the Commission said.
The problems raised most often concerned social security and welfare benefits, taxation and recognition of qualifications.
The start of the campaign was most low-key in the "Eurosceptical" countries Britain and Denmark.
Reflecting this, both those countries scored low in terms of the number of telephone calls to Citizens First, while the highest response levels were in Italy, France, Spain and Germany.

The open market where goods, people, services and capital should have been able to move freely from January 1, 1993, has often been criticised for being business-oriented and for ignoring ordinary citizens.
The European Commission has argued that ordinary people often do not make use of the Union because they are unaware of what it can do for them as it has been badly explained.
